title.en: Izanagi Slays the Fire God Kagutsuchi
title.zh: 伊耶那岐斬火神迦具土

region.en: Mount Hiba, Izumo-Hahaki boundary (symbolic pin, Izumo coordinates; grave of Izanami and scene of the fire god's slaying)
region.zh: 出雲與伯耆交界之比婆山（象徵性標記，採出雲座標；伊耶那美葬地與斬火神場景）

summary.en: Izanami dies giving birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi, whose burning consumes her; grief-stricken Izanagi buries her on Mount Hiba, then draws his ten-grasp sabre and cuts off his child's head. Deities of rock, torrent and spring spring from the blood on the blade, and eight mountain deities are born from the slain god's head, chest, belly, hands and feet.
summary.zh: 伊耶那美因生火神迦具土而陰部被灼身亡；伊耶那岐悲慟葬妻於比婆山，隨即拔十握劍斬下其子之頭。劍刃濺血生出磐裂、根裂等神，迦具土屍身頭、胸、腹、手、足各生山神，化為日本群山之地貌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative still revered in Japan); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Chamberlain translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the Fire-Burning-Swift-Male Deity, Kagutsuchi, was born, the burning of the child consumed his mother's private parts, and Izanami lay sick and dying. Even her sickness was generative: from her vomit were born the Metal-Mountain deities, from her faeces the Clay deities, and from her urine the Water deities, whose child was the Luxuriant-Food-Princess. Then the Female-Who-Invites divinely retired, and Izanagi, wrung with grief, cried that he had exchanged his beloved wife for this single child. As he crept round her pillow and her feet weeping, a weeping female deity was born from his tears, and he buried Izanami on Mount Hiba at the boundary of Izumo and Hahaki.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 115-117 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then grief turned to rage. Izanagi drew the ten-grasp sabre girded at his side, the sword named Heavenly-Point-Blade-Extended, and cut off the head of his child the Fire-Shining-Elder. From the blood that stuck to the point of the august sword and bespattered the multitudinous rock-masses were born the Rock-Splitter, the Root-Splitter and the Rock-Possessing-Male Deity. From the blood on the upper blade came the Awfully-Swift Deity, the Fire-Swift Deity and the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male Deity; and from the blood that collected on the hilt and leaked between Izanagi's fingers came Kura-okami and Kura-mitsuha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 117-119 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The slain fire god's own body proved no less fertile. From his head was born the Possessor-of-the-True-Pass-Mountains; from his chest, the Possessor-of-Descent-Mountains; from his belly, the Possessor-of-the-Innermost Mountains; from his private parts, the Possessor-of-the-Dark-Mountains; from his left and right hands, the Possessors of the Dense and Outlying Mountains; and from his left and right feet, the Possessors of the Moorland and Outer Mountains. Thus the dismembered fire deity, cut apart part by part from head to foot, peopled the mountains of Japan with their divine lords.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 119-120 (1882); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The fire god Kagutsuchi — the Fire-Burning-Swift-Male Deity, Fire-Shining-Prince, Fire-Shining-Elder — was the last-born child of the creator pair Izanagi and Izanami, and his birth destroyed his mother. As the child passed through her, his burning consumed her private parts, and Izanami lay down sick unto death. Even her sickness was generative: from her vomit were born the deities of the metal mountains; from her faeces, the deities of clay; from her urine, the water deities, whose child was the Luxuriant-Food-Princess. Then the Female-Who-Invites divinely retired — the Kojiki's phrase for the death of a deity — and Izanagi lost the partner with whom he had made the islands of Japan.

His grief was extravagant. He clung to the body, crept round her pillow and her feet, and wept, and from his tears was born a weeping female deity who dwells on Mount Kagu near Unewo. 'Oh, thine Augustness, my lovely younger sister! Oh, that I should have exchanged thee for this single child!' he cried — a child valued against a wife. Then he buried Izanami on Mount Hiba, on the boundary between the lands of Izumo and Hahaki, and her grave-mountain stands there in the mythic geography of Japan.

Grief curdled into rage against the child who had cost him his wife. Izanagi drew the ten-grasp sabre girded on him — its names recorded as Heavenly-Point-Blade-Extended and Majestic-Point-Blade-Extended — and cut off the head of the fire god.

But in this myth nothing dies without giving birth. From the blood that clung to the point of the sword and spattered the multitudinous rock-masses sprang three deities: the Rock-Splitter, the Root-Splitter and the Rock-Possessing-Male Deity, lords of bedrock and quarry. From the blood that clung to the upper blade and again bespattered the rocks came three more: the Awfully-Swift Deity, the Fire-Swift Deity and the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male Deity, with his alternative names Brave-Snapping and Luxuriant-Snapping. From the blood that collected on the hilt and leaked out between Izanagi's fingers were born Kura-okami and Kura-mitsuha, dragons of the valleys and springs from whom old priestly houses traced their descent.

The slain god's own body was no less fertile. From his head was born the Possessor-of-the-True-Pass-Mountains; from his chest, the Possessor-of-Descent-Mountains; from his belly, the Possessor-of-the-Innermost Mountains; from his private parts, the Possessor-of-the-Dark-Mountains; from his left hand, the Possessor-of-the-Dense Mountains; from his right hand, the Possessor-of-the-Outlying-Mountains; from his left foot, the Possessor-of-the-Moorland-Mountains; and from his right foot, the Possessor-of-the-Outer-Mountains. Eight mountain deities, mapped onto the corpse part by part from head to foot, took lordship over Japan's mountain landscape — the passes, the inner depths, the dark defiles, the wooded slopes, the moorland heights.

Comparative mythologists have long set this episode beside the great dismemberment cosmogonies: Ymir, hacked apart by Odin and his brothers so that his flesh became the earth and his skull the sky; Tiamat, split by Marduk and halved into heaven and sea; Pangu, whose body became the world at his death; the Vedic Purusha, whose sacrificed limbs yielded the social classes and the beasts of sacrifice. The Kagutsuchi episode is the Japanese member of that cluster, with a characteristic twist: the dismembered being is not a primordial giant who already contained the world, but a young god of the element that most terrifies rice-farmers — fire. And the world created from his parts is not the cosmos itself but the specific, practical geography of mountains, rocks and water that a mountainous archipelago lives from. The blood spilled in the slaying generates not social orders but raw terrain: rock, cliff, torrent, spring, wooded height and moor.

The episode also does quieter work in the Kojiki's larger plot. It supplies the motive — Izanami's death — that sends Izanagi down to Yomi, where he will break the taboo of looking and bring death's permanence into the world. It supplies the first of the great divine swords: the blade that severed Kagutsuchi is the ancestor of the ten-grasp sabre Susanoo carries, the sword with which he slays the eight-headed serpent, and from whose tail the Herb-Quelling Great Sword of the imperial regalia is drawn. And it institutes the principle that violence toward the gods is cosmologically productive: Susanoo's own rampage and the slaying of the food goddess Ogetsuhime, which brings forth rice, millet and beans, repeat the same pattern in a later generation.

Ritually, the story underwrites the mountain cults of Japan — the mountain deities, lords of passes, forests and moors, who receive worship from foresters, hunters and mountain villages — and the dragon-deities of valley water from whom notable priestly clans claimed descent. It frames fire as both indispensable and murderous: Kagutsuchi must exist, for he is the origin of fire in the world, yet must be slain, for his uncontrolled force burns even the gods. In later Shinto fire-rituals the dangerous fire is ritually split and pacified, a pattern that readers have traced back to this mythic cutting-up of the fire god.

functions: Etiological charter for Japan's mountain cults: eight mountain lords from the slain god's body map the mythic geography of passes, forests, cliffs and moors, and underwrite worship of mountain deities by foresters, hunters and mountain communities.
Explains and tames the terror of fire: the indispensable but murderous fire element must be divided and pacified, a pattern echoed in later Shinto fire-calming rites.
Ancestral genealogy: the blood deities born from the sword were claimed as founders by old water-clan and priestly lineages, welding local cults into the imperial myth-cycle.
Narrative hinge of the Kojiki's first book: Izanami's death at Kagutsuchi's birth sends Izanagi to Yomi, bringing death into the world, and passes the ten-grasp sword on to Susanoo's later deeds.

variants.name: Nihongi version: Kagutsuchi cut into five pieces
variants.text_tradition: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Book I, 'One writing says...' (trans. Aston 1896)
variants.summary: The Nihongi variant has Izanagi cut the fire god into five pieces, which become deities, while the blood on the sword likewise begets gods and the blade itself is revered as a deity; the emphasis falls on the divinity of the sword rather than the geography of the corpse.

variants.name: Norse: Ymir slain by Odin, Vili and Ve
variants.text_tradition: Prose Edda and Voluspa (Icelandic, c. 1220s / c. 1270s manuscripts)
variants.summary: The primordial giant Ymir is killed and his flesh becomes the earth, his blood the sea, his bones the mountains, his skull the sky — the classic dismemberment cosmogony parallel to Kagutsuchi's limbs becoming mountains.

variants.name: Babylonian: Marduk splits Tiamat
variants.text_tradition: Enuma Elish (Babylonian, c. late 2nd millennium BCE)
variants.summary: Marduk slays the chaos-mother Tiamat and splits her like a shellfish into heaven and earth, her waters forming the world — a combat-dismemberment creation parallel.

variants.name: Chinese: Pangu's body becomes the world
variants.summary: The giant Pangu, who separated heaven and earth, dies and his body transforms into mountains, rivers, wind, clouds and stars — like Kagutsuchi, a dissolved body yields the landscape.

variants.name: Vedic: the sacrifice of Purusha
variants.summary: The primeval man Purusha is offered up and dismembered; from his parts come the social classes, animals and the worlds — the ritual-dissection parallel to the Kagutsuchi blood-and-limb births.

title.en: Izanagi Divides the Realm: Susanoo's Weeping and Expulsion
title.zh: 伊耶那岐命三子分治與須佐之男命哭泣被逐

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki - symbolic pin)
region.zh: 高天原（宮崎高千穗高原，象徵性標記）

summary.en: Washing after his return from the land of the dead, Izanagi begets three illustrious children and divides the cosmos among them: Amaterasu the sun rules Heaven, Tsukuyomi the night, Susanoo the sea. Susanoo refuses his charge and weeps until mountains wither and seas dry, and his father expels him with a divine expulsion.
summary.zh: 伊耶那岐自黃泉歸來後於日向洗滌己身，洗面而生三貴子：天照大神治高天原，月讀命治夜之國，須佐之男命治海原。須佐之男命不受命，哭嚎至鬚長八握，青山枯萎、河海乾涸，遂被父神以神逐驅逐。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After fleeing the polluted land of Yomi, Izanagi purified himself in a river-mouth near Tachibana in Himuka. As he washed his face, three illustrious children were born: from his left eye the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, Amaterasu; from his right eye the Moon-Night-Possessor, Tsukuyomi; and from his nose the Brave-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness, Susanoo. Rejoicing that his final begetting had produced three illustrious children, Izanagi jingled off his necklace, named it the August-Storehouse-Shelf-Deity, hung it on Amaterasu and charged her to rule the Plain of High Heaven; to Tsukuyomi he gave the Dominion of the Night; and to Susanoo the Sea-Plain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 128-130 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi each assumed their rule, but Susanoo did not. He wept and howled until his eight-grasp beard reached the pit of his stomach, withering the green mountains and drying up all the rivers and seas, while the sound of bad deities swarmed like the flies of the fifth month and every portent of woe arose. Asked why he wept instead of ruling the land he had been charged with, he answered that he wished to depart to his deceased mother's land, the Nether Distant Land. Enraged, Izanagi declared that he should not dwell in this land, and expelled him with a divine expulsion; then Izanagi retired to dwell at Taga in Afumi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 130-131 (1882); not verbatim.

title.zh: 須佐之男命與天照大神的誓約

region.en: Tranquil River of Heaven, Plain of High Heaven (Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki - symbolic pin)
region.zh: 天安川，高天原（宮崎高千穗高原，象徵性標記）

summary.en: Expelled from his father's realm, Susanoo ascends to heaven to take leave of his sister; suspecting invasion, Amaterasu arms herself in war-gear and challenges him. To prove his sincerity they swear an oath on opposite banks of the Tranquil River of Heaven, crunching each other's jewels and sword and blowing the fragments away as deities — three females from his blade, five males from her jewels.
summary.zh: 須佐之男命被逐後上高天原辭別姊姊天照大神；天照疑其來意不善，束髮佩玉、執弓負箭嚴陣相待。二神乃立於天安川兩岸誓約，互取對方之劍玉咬嚼吹氣而生神：其劍生三女神（多紀理毘賣等），其玉生五男神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Expelled from his father's realm, Susanoo resolved to take leave of his sister before departing, and his ascent shook all the mountains and rivers, so that every land quaked. Amaterasu, alarmed, declared his intent surely no good and readied for war: she unbound her hair, twisted it into bunches, threaded strings of curved jewels through hair, head-dress and both arms, slung a quiver of a thousand arrows and another of five hundred, brandished her bow, stamped her feet into the hard ground up to her thighs, kicking away the earth like rotten snow, and stood valiantly like a mighty man, demanding wherefore he had ascended. Susanoo swore he had no evil intent, only a wish to take leave, and proposed that each of them swear an oath and produce children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 131-133 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: On opposite banks of the Tranquil River of Heaven they performed the ordeal. Amaterasu begged Susanoo's ten-grasp sabre, broke it into three fragments, washed and crunched the pieces with her jewels in the True-Pool-Well of Heaven, and blew the mist away, begetting three female deities: Torrent-Mist-Princess, Lovely-Island-Princess and Princess-of-the-Torrent — the three great deities of the Munakata shrines. Susanoo then begged her five strings of jewels from her hair, head-dress and arms, crunched them one by one and blew the mist away, begetting five male deities, among them the Truly-Conqueror-I-Conquer-Conquering-Swift-Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears and Ame-no-hohi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 133-136 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Amaterasu declared the division: the five male deities were born from things of hers, so they were undoubtedly her children; the three female deities were born from a thing of his, so they were doubtless his. But Susanoo, impetuous with what he took for victory — had he not, from his own sword, begotten delicate females? — grew reckless, and the oath that should have sealed his good faith instead opened the season of his outrages in heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 136-138 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Susanoo Ravages Heaven and Is Punished
title.zh: 須佐之男命肆虐高天原被罰

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki - symbolic pin; ends with expulsion toward Torikami, Izumo)
region.zh: 高天原（宮崎高千穗高原，象徵性標記；終於被逐往出雲鳥髮）

summary.en: Convinced his oath contest proved victory, Susanoo wrecked his sister's heaven: breaking the rice-field ridges, filling ditches, fouling the food-palace, and dropping a backward-flayed heavenly horse into the weaving-hall, where a startled weaving woman was killed by her shuttle. For these crimes the eight hundred myriad deities fined him a thousand tables, cut his beard, pulled his nails, and expelled him.
summary.zh: 須佐之男命自以誓約得勝，於高天原大肆破壞：毀天照大神之田埂、填溝渠、於大嘗殿污穢，又於織殿頂破洞，倒剝天之斑駒投入，織女受驚為梭所擊而死。八百萬神乃議罰，令其設千座贖罪、剃鬚拔手足爪，以神逐驅逐之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Judging from the delicate females his oath had produced, Susanoo concluded he had gained the victory, and, impetuous with victory, wrecked his sister's realm. He broke down the divisions of the rice-fields Amaterasu had laid out, filled up the ditches, and strewed excrement in the palace where she partook of the great food. Amaterasu upbraided him not, excusing him: what looked like filth must be what her elder brother had vomited through drunkenness, and his wrecking of the fields must be his grudge for the land. But he only continued his evil acts, more and more violent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 138-139 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last, while Amaterasu sat in her weaving-hall seeing to the weaving of the august garments of the deities, Susanoo broke a hole in the top of the hall and through it let fall a heavenly piebald horse which he had flayed backwards. The women weaving the heavenly garments were so much alarmed at the sight that one of them struck her private parts against the shuttle and died. This outrage drove the sun goddess to hide in the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling, and the whole plain of heaven and the Central Land of Reed-Plains went dark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 139-140 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she had been brought out of the rock-dwelling and light returned, the eight hundred myriad deities took counsel together and punished Susanoo: they imposed on him a fine of a thousand tables of offerings, cut off his beard, and caused the nails of his fingers and toes to be pulled out, expelling him with a divine expulsion. So the storm god, shorn of beard and nails, descended from the Plain of High Heaven to Torikami at the head-waters of the River Hi in the land of Izumo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 145-146 (1882); not verbatim.

title.zh: 大宜都比賣之死與五穀起源

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki - symbolic pin)
region.zh: 高天原（宮崎高千穗高原，象徵性標記）

summary.en: Expelled from heaven, Susanoo begs food of the goddess Princess-of-Great-Food; seeing her draw dainties from her own nose, mouth and fundament, he judges it filth and kills her. From the slain goddess's body spring silkworms, rice, millet and beans, which the Deity-Producing-Wondrous-Ancestor causes to be used as seed — the origin of cultivated food.
summary.zh: 須佐之男命被逐後向大宜都比賣神乞食；女神自鼻、口乃至穢處取出珍饌調成諸餚奉上。須佐之男命窺其所為，疑其以穢物相饗，遂殺之。其屍身頭生蠶，目生稻種，耳生粟，鼻生小豆，陰生麥，穀生大豆；神產巢日御祖命皆取為種，是為五穀蠶桑之起源。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Expelled from heaven, Susanoo begged food of the Deity Princess-of-Great-Food, Ogetsuhime. She took out all sorts of dainty things from her nose, her mouth and even her fundament, and made them up into all sorts of dishes, which she offered to him. But Susanoo watched her proceedings, considered that she was offering up filth to him, and at once killed the goddess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain page 145 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the body of the slain goddess food sprang for the world: silkworms were born in her head, rice seeds in her two eyes, millet in her two ears, small beans in her nose, barley in her private parts and large beans in her fundament. The Deity-Producing-Wondrous-Ancestor had them all taken and used as seed, so that the killing of the food goddess became the origin of the crops and the silkworms that feed and clothe humankind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 145-146 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Susanoo Builds the Palace of Suga

summary.en: After slaying the eight-forked serpent, Susanoo seeks a place to build his palace and arrives at Suga in Izumo, where his heart feels pure; clouds rise as he builds, and he sings the first waka of the Kojiki, the eight-fold fence song. He appoints the old man Foot-Stroking-Elder head of his palace and marries his daughter, the rescued Wondrous-Inada-Princess, begetting the Deity Eight-Island-Ruler.
summary.zh: 須佐之男命斬八岐大蛇後，於出雲覓地造宮，行至須賀，曰「吾心清淨」，遂建宮殿，雲氣騰起，乃詠「八雲立出雲八重垣」之歌。以足名椎為宮之長，娶其獲救之女櫛名田比賣為妻，於新婚之室生八島士奴美神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After cutting the eight-forked serpent to pieces, Susanoo sought in the land of Izumo for a place where he might build a palace. He arrived at a place called Suga and said: 'On coming to this place my august heart is pure.' There he built a palace to dwell in, and that place is called Suga to this day. When the Great Deity first built the palace of Suga, clouds rose up from it, and he made an august song: 'The eight-fold clouds of Izumo arise to make an eight-fold fence about my wife within the eight-fold fence — a wondrous eight-fold fence indeed.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 149-151 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: There Susanoo called the old man Foot-Stroking-Elder and appointed him head-man of his palace, and took as his wife the Wondrous-Inada-Princess, the daughter whom the serpent had been about to devour. In their bridal chamber they begot a child, the Deity Eight-Island-Ruler, from whom — so the record traces — the line of the Great-Name-Possessor, Master of the Great Land, was descended. Thus the serpent-slayer settled the land of Izumo, founding lord of its palace, song and shrines.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 151-152 (1882); not verbatim.
